known_incidents: The survey drone Certainty was sent into the anomaly's core in 2612; telemetry showed its hull losing molecular cohesion over 47 minutes before the signal dissolved into static—final readings suggested the drone's matter had become a quantum probability cloud.

In 2641, a salvage crew working the boundary accidentally exposed a cargo container to the transition zone; the container's steel walls flowed like liquid for six seconds before resolidifying into an unknown crystalline alloy now worth more than the ship that carried it.
description: Velvet Dissolution appears as a softly luminous fog of impossible color—iridescent, shifting, as if reality itself has become uncertain about what it should look like. Starlight entering the anomaly doesn't emerge on the other side; it simply stops being light and becomes something else, something sensors can detect but cannot classify. The fog is beautiful in the way that deep ocean bioluminescence is beautiful: mesmerizing, alien, and a reminder that you are in a place where the rules you depend on no longer apply.

The anomaly is expanding. Slowly, chaotically, but measurably, the Velvet Dissolution grows—2 to 8 kilometers per year, its boundary oscillating unpredictably. At the transition zone, matter loses its certainty. Metals soften, ceramics flow, and the crisp boundaries between solid and liquid and gas become suggestions rather than laws. Objects don't explode or burn; they dissolve, gently and completely, their molecules losing the quantum coherence that gives matter its structure. The process is eerily quiet. There is no violence in dissolution—only absence.

No one knows what created the Velvet Dissolution or how long it has existed. Its expansion suggests it is either young and growing or ancient and accelerating, but dating an anomaly that destroys the evidence of its own age is problematic. The loss of the Certainty drone in 2612 provided the most detailed data to date: 47 minutes of telemetry showing matter transitioning from solid to probabilistic, each atom becoming a smeared wave function rather than a particle. The scientific community is divided between those who see the Dissolution as the most important physics discovery in centuries and those who see it as an existential threat.

The boundary zone has become a site of extraordinary—and extraordinarily dangerous—industry. The transition between coherent and decoherent matter allows for the creation of materials that cannot exist under normal quantum conditions. The accidental crystalline alloy produced in 2641 has properties that material scientists cannot replicate in any laboratory. Entrepreneurs and researchers work the boundary in heavily shielded vessels, scooping exotic matter and retreating before dissolution claims their ships. The margins are razor-thin. And every year, the Velvet Dissolution grows a little larger, its beautiful fog reaching outward, patient and gentle and utterly annihilating.
